# Penguin

> Penguin is a funny pedometer and step counter app for iPhone (on the App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/penguin-step-counter-pedometer/id6831137240), published by Lightbulb Moment Labs, Inc. Your daily steps from Apple Health power a smug, overconfident cartoon penguin. It's "the pedometer for people who hate pedometers." Now on the App Store.

Key facts:
- Platform: iPhone (iOS). Counts steps from Apple Health, so it works with just a phone or with an Apple Watch.
- Reads step count only. Step history stays on the device. No accounts, ads, analytics, or tracking.
- The penguin starts out pudgy (the couch bird) and gets fitter as you walk: couch bird, strong waddler, then athlete. It's framed as strength and confidence, never weight, and he never comments on the user's body.
- Daily step goal with rest days that never cost progress ("Aura").
- The Locker: unlockable outfits. Most are earned by walking; Penguin Plus adds Plus-only fits.
- Expeditions: an endless map of landmarks unlocked by steps.
- Waddles: small friend groups that share goal progress through iCloud and can send pokes.
- Pricing: free to download. The free version counts every step and includes the full glow-up, Aura, streaks, Waddles, widgets, and the first expedition. Penguin Plus ($39.99/year or $9.99/month, 7-day free trial on the yearly plan) adds monthly drops of new fits, every expedition after the first (11 and counting, then endless victory laps), Plus-only fits, and Waddle challenges (weekend step races and group goals; friends join free). Coming to Plus: a monthly Walk Wrapped recap, and customization (app icons, widget themes).
- Contact: gary@penguinathletics.com

## Learn: the health benefits of walking
Evidence-based, cited articles. Editorial policy: https://penguinathletics.com/learn/editorial-policy/

- [Walking and your heart](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-heart-health/): Blood pressure, cholesterol, and the most underrated cardio on the planet.
- [Walking and longevity](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-longevity/): How many steps buy you more years, and what the 10,000-step rule gets wrong.
- [Walking for weight loss](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-weight-loss/): What walking really does for weight, blood sugar, and metabolism. No shame, just science.
- [Walking and your mind](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-mental-health/): Stress, mood, sleep, and focus. A walk is the cheapest reset you own.
- [Walking basics](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-basics/): How to start, stick with it, and maybe even like it. Built for people who hate exercise.

- [Is it too late to start walking at 60?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/is-it-too-late-to-start-walking-at-60/): No, it isn't too late. Large studies link becoming more active in midlife and later to a lower risk of early death, and a review of adults 60 and older linked even small amounts of moderate activity to a 22% lower risk. In a trial of adults aged 70 to 89, a walking-based program lowered the risk of losing the ability to walk about a quarter mile.
- [Can walking reduce belly fat?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/can-walking-reduce-belly-fat/): Yes, a little. In trials where walking was the only change, waist size shrank by about 1.5 cm on average, and reviews show regular aerobic exercise like brisk walking can reduce the deep fat around your organs, sometimes without much weight loss. You can't target belly fat with ab exercises, so overall activity and eating habits matter more than any single move.
- [Can walking reduce your risk of stroke?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/can-walking-reduce-your-risk-of-stroke/): Probably, yes. In a review of 7 long-term studies, people who walked fastest had a 44% lower risk of stroke than people who walked slowest, and older men who walked more hours each week had fewer strokes. These studies show a strong link rather than proof, but walking also lowers blood pressure, the biggest risk factor for stroke.
- [Does walking help you sleep better?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/does-walking-help-you-sleep-better/): Yes, for many people it does. A 2026 review of 21 trials found that regular walking improved self-reported sleep quality in adults, with the biggest gains in people who slept worst to start with. The certainty is still low, and walking works best alongside proven insomnia treatment, not instead of it.
- [How to walk with good posture](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/how-to-walk-with-good-posture/): Stand tall, keep your chin level and your eyes about 10 to 20 feet ahead, relax your shoulders down and back, let your arms swing naturally, and roll smoothly from heel to toe without overstriding. Letting your arms swing matters: holding them still took about 12% more energy in one lab study. There's no single perfect posture, so aim for comfortable and relaxed, not rigid.
- [Walking speed and life expectancy: what's the link?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-speed-and-life-expectancy-what-s-the-link/): People who naturally walk faster tend to live longer. In a pooled study of 34,485 adults 65 and older, each 0.1 meter per second of extra walking speed was linked to a 12% lower risk of death, and speeds of about 1.0 meter per second (around 2.2 mph) or faster went with longer-than-expected survival. Speed is partly a sign of overall health, so it shows a strong link rather than proof that walking faster adds years.
- [Does walking after meals lower blood sugar?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/does-walking-after-meals-lower-blood-sugar/): Yes. Trials show that walking soon after you eat lowers the blood sugar rise that follows a meal. In one trial of adults with type 2 diabetes, a 10-minute walk after each main meal lowered after-meal blood sugar about 12% more than a single daily 30-minute walk, and about 22% more after dinner.
- [Does walking lower cholesterol?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/does-walking-lower-cholesterol/): A little, but the evidence is mixed. A review of 25 trials found regular walking lowered LDL ("bad") cholesterol by about 5%, while a later review of 32 walking trials found no clear change in blood fats. Walking helps your heart in other proven ways, but on its own it usually won't fix high cholesterol.
- [How does walking reduce stress?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/how-walking-reduces-stress/): Walking seems to ease stress in a few ways. Regular physical activity reduces psychological distress in trials, and active people tend to have a healthier daily cortisol rhythm. Time outdoors adds to it: in one study, 20 to 30 minutes in nature gave the biggest drop in the stress hormone cortisol for the time spent.
- [What's the best time of day to walk?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/best-time-of-day-to-walk/): There's no single best time. Large studies disagree, linking morning, midday, and evening activity to lower risks, and walking at any time of day is linked to a longer life. If you want a tiebreaker, a 10-minute walk after each meal lowered after-meal blood sugar about 12% more than one daily 30-minute walk in a trial of adults with type 2 diabetes.
- [How many steps a day to lose weight?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/how-many-steps-a-day-to-lose-weight/): There's no single step count that guarantees weight loss. In a 2026 review of weight-loss trials, people who raised their steps to about 8,500 a day and stayed there kept more weight off, but the extra steps didn't speed up the initial loss. Walking on its own usually leads to modest weight loss, so steps work best alongside eating changes.
- [Walking vs running: which is better for your heart?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-vs-running-which-is-better-for-your-heart/): Both are good for your heart, and neither clearly wins. In a study of about 49,000 walkers and runners, burning the same amount of energy by walking or running led to similar drops in the risk of high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, and possibly heart disease. Running gets you there in less time, while walking takes longer but is easier to start and stick with.
- [Is walking good for depression?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/is-walking-good-for-depression/): Yes, walking can help. A 2024 review of 44 trials in adults found walking reduced depression symptoms compared with not walking, and the effect was bigger in people who were already depressed. Walking works best as part of your care, alongside therapy or medication when you need them, not as a replacement.
- [What is a good daily step goal?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/what-is-a-good-daily-step-goal/): There's no single magic number. Large studies link about 7,000 steps a day to much lower health risks than 2,000, with benefits leveling off around 6,000 to 8,000 steps for adults 60 and older and 8,000 to 10,000 for younger adults. The best personal goal starts from your current daily average and climbs a little at a time.
- [Is the 10,000 steps rule real?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/is-the-10000-steps-rule-real/): The 10,000 steps rule is not based on science. It traces back to a marketing campaign in Japan. Large studies find health benefits start at as few as about 2,500 steps a day, with the drop in risk of early death leveling off at around 7,000 to 9,000 steps for most adults, though 10,000 is still a fine goal if you can reach it.
- [How many calories does walking burn?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/how-many-calories-does-walking-burn/): A 30-minute brisk walk uses roughly 140 to 240 calories for most adults, and in one study, walking a mile used about 90 to 110 calories. The biggest factors are your body weight, your pace, and whether you're going uphill. Every calorie number, including the one on your watch, is an estimate, so treat it as a rough guide.
- [Walking for weight loss: the complete guide](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-weight-loss/): Walking on its own usually leads to modest weight loss. In a review of pedometer-based walking programs with no diet changes, people lost about 1.3 kg (roughly 3 pounds) over a median of 16 weeks. Walking does more when paired with changes in eating, and it helps prevent weight gain and improves blood sugar and insulin sensitivity whatever the scale says.
- [Walking and your mind: the complete guide](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-mental-health/): Walking is good for your mental health. A 2024 review of 75 trials found that walking reduced symptoms of depression and anxiety in adults, and people who move more tend to have a lower risk of depression. Walking works best alongside therapy or medication when you need them, not instead of them.
- [Walking and longevity: the complete guide](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-longevity/): People who walk more tend to live longer. In a 2025 review of 57 studies, 7,000 steps a day was linked to a 47% lower risk of early death compared with 2,000 steps, and the benefits started to level off around 5,000 to 7,000 steps. Most of this evidence is observational, so it shows a strong link rather than proof, but walking is also linked to lower dementia risk and better function as you age.
- [Walking and your heart: the complete guide](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-heart-health/): Walking is one of the best-studied ways to help your heart. In trials it lowered systolic blood pressure by about 4 mmHg, and in long-term studies people who walked the most had about 31% lower risk of cardiovascular disease than people who walked the least. Aim for about 150 minutes a week at a brisk pace, and start smaller if you need to.
- [Walking basics: the complete beginner's guide](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/walking-basics/): Adults need at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, and brisk walking counts. That's about 30 minutes a day, five days a week, at a pace where you can talk but not sing. If you're starting from zero, any amount helps, so begin small and build up gradually.
- [How to start walking when you hate exercise](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/how-to-start-walking-when-you-hate-exercise/): Start smaller than you think you need to, like a 5 to 10 minute walk tied to something you already do every day, and add a few minutes each week. Health guidelines say some activity is better than none and short walks count. New habits took about 66 days on average to feel automatic in one study, so aim for consistency, not intensity.
- [How many steps a day to live longer?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/how-many-steps-a-day-to-live-longer/): In a pooled analysis of 15 studies, the risk of dying early kept falling as steps rose, then leveled off at about 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day for adults 60 and older and 8,000 to 10,000 for younger adults. You don't need 10,000 to benefit: a 2025 review linked 7,000 steps a day to a 47% lower risk of death than 2,000 steps.
- [How many steps a day do you need for heart health?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/how-many-steps-a-day-do-you-need-for-heart-health/): You probably don't need 10,000. In large studies, people who took more steps had a lower risk of heart disease, with most of the benefit showing up by about 7,000 to 9,000 steps a day. In adults 60 and older, 6,000 to 9,000 steps a day was linked to a 40% to 50% lower risk of heart disease than about 2,000 steps.
- [Does walking lower blood pressure?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/does-walking-lower-blood-pressure/): Yes. A large Cochrane review of 73 trials found that regular walking lowered systolic blood pressure (the top number) by about 4 mmHg on average. Most of the walking programs in those trials averaged around 150 minutes of moderate walking a week for a few months.
- [Does walking help anxiety?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/does-walking-help-anxiety/): Yes, for many people it helps. A 2024 review of 26 trials in adults found that regular walking reduced anxiety symptoms compared with doing nothing, and a single bout of exercise can bring a small short-term drop too. Walking works best alongside therapy or medication when you need them, not instead of them.
- [Can you lose weight just by walking?](https://penguinathletics.com/learn/can-you-lose-weight-just-by-walking/): Yes, but usually only a little. In trials of walking alone, people lost about 1.4 kg (roughly 3 pounds) on average, and programs that combine walking with eating changes lead to more weight loss. Walking still improves blood pressure, blood sugar, and fitness even when the scale barely moves.
